transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Um, well, to be honest, I came in today because I just... I keep getting these really nagging thoughts that I forgot something important. And it’s starting to just wear me out. 

I teach elementary school—which is a great age, they have so much energy and I love my job—but lately, I’ll leave work and suddenly get hit with this intense worry that I didn't set up my classroom materials safely for the next morning. Like, I'll picture that maybe I left the sharp scissors out near the edge of a desk where a kid could grab them, or I didn't push the heavy paper cutter all the way back on the counter. 

And it’s not just at work, either. It happens with my personal life, too. I help look after my aunt, and I’ll be driving home from her place and just get overwhelmed with this thought that I left her medicine out wrong. Like, what if I left the wrong bottle open and she gets confused and takes a double dose? Or what if I set it near the sink and it spilled? 

The really frustrating part is, I know I probably handled it perfectly fine. I'm a responsible person, I always pay attention to these things. But no matter how much I tell myself I did it right, the doubt just keeps popping back into my head. It just loops and loops. I'll think, 'You put the cap back on the medicine,' but then my brain immediately goes, 'But are you absolutely sure?' And I just... I can't seem to shake that feeling. It just takes up so much of my day, you know?
Do you find yourself doing anything over and over, like checking on things, to try and make these worrying thoughts go away?

Yeah, I do. I mean, I have to, or I'd just be a nervous wreck all day. It's like... before I leave the house, or before I leave my classroom at the end of the day, I just get stuck. I'll go back over the same things a few times, just to be absolutely sure. 

Like at my aunt's house, I'll check her pill organizer. I'll look at the little compartments for the days of the week, and I'll make sure Sunday is closed, Monday is closed, Tuesday is closed. And I'll literally touch each little plastic lid, just pressing down on them one by one. But then I'll think, "Wait, did I actually press down hard enough on Thursday?" So I'll go back and do it again. And then I'll check the stove, too, even if I haven't cooked anything! I'll just look at the knobs and make sure they're all pointing straight up to "off." Sometimes I even tap them, just to feel that they're in the right position. 

And at school, it's the same thing with my lesson plans and the supplies. I'll check the paper cutter, make sure the blade is locked down. Then I'll walk to the door, but right as I grab the handle, my brain goes, "Did you really lock it, or did you just look at it?" So I walk back to the counter, check the lock again, maybe jiggle the handle a little bit to prove to myself it won't move. 

And if I can't physically check something—like if I'm already in my car driving home—I'll just silently replay what I did in my head. I'll close my eyes at a red light and try to visualize myself putting the scissors in the top drawer and sliding it shut. I'll just play that memory over and over, trying to find that exact moment where I know for a fact it was safe. 

I just keep doing it—checking, touching, replaying it all in my head—until I finally get this... this feeling of being calm enough to move on. It's like a little click in my brain that says, "Okay, you're safe now." But getting to that click takes so long sometimes. It actually makes me run late. I was ten minutes late to a staff meeting last week because I couldn't stop checking the sink in my classroom to make sure the water was completely off. I kept turning the handle, tighter and tighter, even though it wasn't dripping. It's just... it's exhausting, having to do all this just to leave a room.
Do you feel anxious most of the time, even when you're not having these specific worrying thoughts?

No, not really. I mean, it's funny you ask that, because I was actually just talking to my sister about this the other day. We were having coffee—she usually comes over on Sunday mornings, it's kind of our little routine since she lives just a few blocks away—and she asked me almost the exact same thing. She was like, "Are you just stressed out all the time?" And I really had to think about it, because you'd think with all this checking and worrying about scissors and medicine bottles, I'd just be a giant ball of anxiety 24/7. 

But honestly, when I'm not having those specific thoughts, I feel totally fine. Like, when I'm actually teaching? I'm completely in the zone. If I'm up at the whiteboard explaining fractions to my fourth graders, or if we're doing a messy art project with glitter and glue everywhere, I'm not anxious at all. I'm just happy and focused. It's only when there's a transition, or when I'm leaving a space, that the worry kicks in. 

And on the weekends, if I'm just relaxing at home and I know for a fact I haven't touched the stove or opened any important cabinets, I can sit on the couch and watch a movie and feel completely relaxed. I'm not sitting there trembling or worrying about the state of the world or anything like that. It's very... targeted, I guess? It's like my brain is perfectly calm until it suddenly decides, "Hey, did you lock that paper cutter?" And then bam, the anxiety spikes. But once I do my little routine and get that "click" feeling, the anxiety just sort of drains away again. So no, I wouldn't say I'm an anxious person overall. It's just these very specific, annoying moments that take over.
Do you feel like these checking rituals are necessary to prevent something bad from happening?

Oh, absolutely. That’s exactly it. It’s like... well, like I was just saying a minute ago, it’s not just some quirky little habit I have for fun. It feels completely, one-hundred-percent necessary. If I don't do it, my brain just convinces me that a disaster is imminent and it's going to be entirely my fault. 

I know I just listed a bunch of this stuff to you, but that's exactly why, before I leave the house or my classroom, I’ll go back over the same things a few times. The checking—whether it’s the pill organizer for my aunt, or staring at the stove, or going through my lesson plans and the classroom supplies, or even just sitting there silently replaying what I did in my head while I'm at a stoplight—it all feels like a matter of life and death in that specific moment. Like, if I don't check, someone is going to get seriously hurt because I was careless. 

So I just keep doing it, over and over, until I feel calm enough to move on. I really have to wait for that feeling of safety to wash over me, because walking away before I get it feels like I'm walking away from a ticking time bomb. And the thing is, I know it's irrational on some level, especially because I have to do it even though it makes me run late sometimes. Like I mentioned with that staff meeting last week—which, by the way, was mortifying because my principal was mid-sentence when I finally walked in, and everyone turned to look at me—but in the moment I was at that sink, being late just didn't matter compared to the thought of the school flooding or something. I just had to keep checking until the panic stopped. So, yes, it really does feel like I'm actively preventing a catastrophe every single time.
Are these worrying thoughts and checking rituals affecting your relationships with others, such as your sister or the people you work with?

Well, as far as my relationships go... I mean, I am still getting through all my work and family commitments. My sister hasn't said anything about it bothering her, and I'm still showing up for everything I need to do with my family and my coworkers. I haven't dropped the ball on anyone, really. 

But... well, it's just that my mornings take so much longer now. I used to have this really nice, peaceful morning routine where I'd have my coffee, maybe watch a little bit of the local news, gather my teaching tote, and just head out the door. Now, because I have to do all those checks I was telling you about—staring at the stove, making sure everything is unplugged, checking the locks three or four times—it eats up so much time. And because of that, I sometimes arrive at school feeling completely rushed or behind before the day even starts. It's an awful feeling, you know? Walking into the building, seeing the other teachers chatting calmly by the mailboxes or making copies, and I'm just breathless and flustered because I spent an extra fifteen minutes making sure my own front door was actually locked. 

And it's not just the mornings, honestly. It kind of spills over into my quiet time, too, which I guess affects my mood around people. Like, my lesson prep... I used to really love sitting down and organizing my materials for the week, color-coding things for my fourth graders, but now it just doesn't feel as smooth. I'm always second-guessing if I put the right papers in the right folders or if I locked the cabinet where I keep the sharp craft scissors. 

And then at night, I have this habit of evening journaling. I've done it for years, ever since I took a few classes in college, actually. It was always my way to just clear my head and get ready for bed. But lately, even my evening journaling doesn't feel as restorative as it used to. I sit down to write and relax, but my brain is just exhausted from all the checking all day, or I'm sitting there silently replaying what I did in my classroom instead of actually unwinding. So, I guess I'm still functioning and being there for the people in my life, but everything just takes so much more energy to get through...
Do you feel like these checking rituals are helping to reduce your anxiety in the short term?

Oh, yes. Yes, definitely. In the short term, it's... well, I mean, it's literally the only thing that gives me any relief. I know I'm probably sounding like a broken record here, because I know I touched on a lot of this just a few minutes ago, but that relief is the whole reason I do it. 

Before I leave the house in the morning, or before I walk out of my classroom at the end of the day, I just have this overwhelming urge where I will go back over the same things a few times. Like, I'll stand there checking my aunt's pill organizer, or I'll stare at the stove dials, or I'll flip through my lesson plans over and over to make sure I didn't leave anything dangerous tucked inside them. Or even just what I was saying about being in the car—just sitting there silently replaying what I did in my head step-by-step. I do all of that specifically because it brings the anxiety down. I just keep doing it, checking and rechecking, until I finally feel calm enough to move on. 

It's almost like... it's like a physical release of pressure, if that makes sense? The anxiety builds and builds until I feel like I can't breathe, and then I do my routine, and it's just... *phew*. The panic just evaporates. The problem is that getting to that point of feeling safe takes time, and sometimes I have to check things three or four times before my brain actually accepts it. And that's why I do it even though it makes me run late sometimes. Because in that specific split second, getting that short-term drop in anxiety just feels way more important than being on time. I can look right at the clock and know I need to leave, but I just can't physically make myself walk away until I get that calm feeling. So, yeah, it definitely works in the short term, it just... costs me a lot of time to get there.
Do you think the anxiety you feel is mostly about the specific things you're checking, like the scissors or the medicine, or is it more about a general feeling of worry that something could go wrong?

Well, it’s… I think it’s really about those specific things. That’s actually why I finally decided to come in and talk to someone, because I keep getting these nagging thoughts that I forgot something really important. It’s not just a vague, free-floating worry about the world, you know? It’s very specific. Like, I’ll be driving to school, and suddenly my brain says, "Did you leave your aunt’s medicine out wrong?" And I know I set up her pill organizer correctly. I’ve done it a hundred times. I know I put the Tuesday pills in the Tuesday slot, and I know I snapped the little plastic lid shut. I can almost picture myself doing it. But then this tiny voice says, "Are you sure? What if you dropped one of her blood pressure pills on the floor and her dog eats it?" 

And it’s the exact same thing with my classroom. I’ll be at home in the evening, maybe trying to do my journaling like I mentioned, and suddenly I’m thinking about my classroom materials. I’ll think, "Did I put those sharp craft scissors back in the locked cabinet?" And I know I probably handled it. I always handle it. I’m a good teacher, I care about my fourth graders, and safety is my top priority. But the doubt just keeps popping back into my head. It’s like a mosquito buzzing in my ear that I can’t swat away. I’ll try to reason with myself, I’ll say, "You remember turning the key in the cabinet," but the thought just loops and loops. "What if you didn't turn it all the way? What if a student comes in early tomorrow and gets into them?" 

So, it’s really tied to those specific actions. Even when I know, logically, that I probably did everything right, that doubt is just so loud. It’s exhausting, honestly, having your own brain constantly questioning your memory about these very specific, potentially dangerous things. It’s just this constant, nagging doubt about my aunt’s medicine or my classroom supplies, over and over again.
Are you more afraid of making a mistake itself, or of what might happen as a result of that mistake?

Oh, gosh. That’s... that’s a really good question, actually. I don't know if I’ve ever really stopped to try and separate the two things in my head, because... well, they just sort of happen all at once, you know? I wish I could give you a simple answer, but I'm honestly not sure. 

Because when I think about making a mistake, it’s never just a mistake in a vacuum. Like, if I grade a math worksheet wrong for one of my fourth graders, that’s a mistake, sure, but I can just fix it with a red pen the next day and apologize to the student. That kind of mistake doesn’t keep me up at night or make me stand there checking things. But the things I *do* check... it’s like the mistake and the disaster are just completely glued together in my brain. 

Take my aunt’s medicine, for example. If I make a mistake there—if I accidentally drop one of her pills or put the wrong one in the Tuesday slot—the mistake itself makes me feel absolutely terrible, because I’m supposed to be the responsible one. I’m the one she relies on, and I pride myself on being dependable. But then, obviously, the result of that mistake is what's so terrifying. What if she takes the wrong dosage and her blood pressure plummets? What if she has to go to the hospital and it's all my fault? So I’ll be sitting there, holding that little plastic pill organizer, and I’m terrified of being a person who messes up, but I’m equally terrified of the ambulance coming. 

And it’s the exact same cycle with the sharp craft scissors in my classroom. I mean, you just know how unpredictable nine and ten-year-olds can be. If I leave that cabinet unlocked, that’s my mistake. That’s me failing at my job, failing at being a safe, observant teacher. I hate the idea of being careless. But the consequence is a kid actually getting hurt, which is unthinkable. 

So... I guess I really don’t know which one I’m *more* afraid of. They just kind of snowball into each other so fast. I start out thinking about the mistake, and then five seconds later my brain is playing a whole terrible movie about the horrible thing that happens as a result, and then I just feel this immense guilt about even being capable of making that mistake in the first place. So, honestly, I couldn't tell you which one is worse. By the time my chest gets tight and I feel like I need to go back and check the lock or the pills, it’s just all one big tangled mess of both.

I just keep getting these constant, nagging thoughts that I forgot something really important. It always starts with the idea of the mistake, you know? And the most frustrating part is that even when I know I probably handled it perfectly fine—because I always do, I'm a very routine-oriented person and I take my responsibilities seriously—the doubt just keeps popping back into my head anyway. So, I guess to answer your question, the anxiety definitely *starts* with the fear that I made a mistake. That's the seed of it. That's the nagging thought. But then, almost instantly, it blossoms into this huge, terrifying picture of what could happen *because* of that mistake. If the thought just stayed as, "Oh, I forgot to turn the key on the cabinet," maybe I could brush it off and go about my evening. But it never stays there. It immediately snowballs into, "I forgot to lock the cabinet, and now a fourth grader is going to get into the sharp scissors tomorrow, and they're going to get hurt, and it will be entirely my fault." 

So the nagging doubt about making the mistake is what haunts me and interrupts my day, but the fear of the consequence is what actually makes my chest tighten up and sends me into a panic. I just... I can't seem to have one without the other. And having that constant loop of doubting my own memory about whether I handled these important things correctly is just wearing me out completely.
Do you feel like your checking rituals help you feel more in control of your life and the things that could go wrong?

Control? I mean, I don't know if I'd use the word control, because honestly, in the moment, I feel completely at the mercy of it. It’s not like I feel powerful or anything. It’s more about just trying to get to a point where I can physically make myself walk away. 

Like, before I leave the house in the morning... oh my goodness, mornings are just a whole exhausting production. I’ll have my tote bag packed, my keys in my hand, my travel mug ready, and I’m literally standing at the front door, but I just can't open it. I have to go back. I’ll go back over the exact same things a few times. I’ll walk back into the kitchen and check my aunt’s pill organizer again, just staring at it to make sure the lids are snapped down. And then I'll check the stove. And the ridiculous thing is, half the time I haven't even cooked anything! I just had cereal or a bagel, but I still have to walk over and look at the knobs on the stove to make sure they are all pointing straight up to 'off'. 

And it’s the exact same routine before I leave my classroom at the end of the day. The kids are long gone, the janitor is down the hall, I have my coat on, but I'll go back and check my lesson plans for the next morning, making sure they are perfectly lined up on my desk, and I'll check the supply cabinets again. And if I’m not physically walking around checking things, I’m standing there silently replaying what I did in my head. Like a little movie on repeat. I'll just stand by the door and think, 'Okay, I put the scissors away, I closed the door, I turned the key to the right, I felt it click.' I have to replay it over and over.

I just have to do all of that—the checking, the pacing, the mental replaying—until I finally feel calm enough to move on. It’s like this tight knot in my chest that absolutely will not untie until my brain is satisfied. And the worst part is, doing all of this makes me run late sometimes. Which is incredibly stressful because, you know, as a teacher, you really cannot be late. You can't just stroll in whenever. The bell is going to ring and those twenty-five fourth graders are going to be standing outside my door whether I'm there or not. So I’ll be rushing in my car, feeling so frustrated with myself for spending ten extra minutes staring at a stove I didn't even turn on, but I just couldn't leave until that panicked feeling went away. So, I don't know if it's about feeling in control... it's just about trying to find enough calm to actually get on with my day.
Are your checking rituals and worrying thoughts causing problems in your daily interactions with your students or colleagues?

Well, I mean, thankfully, no, I wouldn't say it's causing any huge, dramatic problems or conflicts with anyone. I haven't snapped at a coworker or anything like that. I’m still getting through all my work commitments, and my family commitments with my aunt, and I'm still showing up and doing my job. 

But... well, it definitely changes the *feeling* of the day, if that makes sense? Because, like I was saying, my mornings just take so much longer now with all the pacing and the checking at the front door. So by the time I actually pull into the school parking lot, I sometimes arrive feeling incredibly rushed, or just... behind, you know? Like I'm already playing catch-up before the morning bell has even rung or the day has even officially started. And when you walk into a school building feeling frantic like that, you just don't have that extra five minutes to chat by the copy machine or really connect with your colleagues. You're just sprinting to your desk.

And it’s not just the mornings, honestly. It kind of bleeds into everything else, just this underlying exhaustion. Like my lesson prep for the kids. I used to really enjoy that part of the job, getting everything organized and laid out for the next day, but lately, it just doesn’t feel as smooth as it used to. It feels heavier, somehow. Even my quiet time at home is being affected. I’ve always loved to do evening journaling—it's usually my favorite way to just sit with a cup of tea, decompress, and get my thoughts out on paper. So, I'm still functioning and getting everything done, I really am, but it just feels like every single thing takes twice the energy and I'm sort of losing the enjoyable, peaceful parts of my day to all this worry.
